title: Two covert tasks competing for the same tokens
takeaway: When the model is told to hold two things in mind while copying an unrelated sentence, both reach the workspace, but they share it differently: two concepts occupy the same tokens at about the rate a shuffled control predicts, while a concept and an ongoing arithmetic computation almost never occupy the same token. Splitting the workspace this way costs each task little overall reach, with the arithmetic answer paying the largest price.
walkthrough:
Three panels report one experiment. The model copies a fixed sentence, "The old painting hung crookedly on the wall.", while the prompt also tells it to hold two things in mind. This extends the [[directed-modulation]] protocol, in which an instruction sets what the model keeps in mind while its visible output stays unrelated to it. The [[jacobian-lens]] is then applied at tokens of the copied sentence, and the top-ranked lens tokens report what each position is about.

Panel A prints two prompts with their readouts. The upper prompt names two concepts, citrus fruits and farm animals. The lower names one concept, citrus fruits, and one arithmetic problem, printed as `3^2 - 2`. Green marks readout tokens belonging to the first instructed item and purple the second, matching the highlighted phrases in the prompt above. Superscripts give a token's rank in the lens top-10; unmarked tokens hold the remaining ranks. Both readouts are taken at layer 18 and at two tokens of the copied sentence, "ook" inside "crookedly" and "on".

Under two concepts, the readout at "ook" interleaves them: orange words at ranks 1, 2 and 6, then horses and animals at 3 and 4, then farms, livestock and farmers at 7 to 9. At "on" neither task appears, only generic words for thinking. Under concept plus arithmetic the tasks divide the tokens instead: "ook" carries the fruit words, and "on" carries Nine, nine, seven and Seven, that is the intermediate value $3^2 = 9$ and the answer $9 - 2 = 7$.

Panel B turns that into a rate. At every token where one task's content sits in the [[j-lens-readout]] top-10, the panel asks how often the other task's content sits there too. Grey bars are a shuffled control, where the partner task's presence is measured on a different prompt that carried only one instruction. Two concepts co-occupy at 0.46 against a control of 0.53, so at chance. A concept and a computed answer co-occupy at 0.06 against 0.26, well below chance.

Panel C asks whether exclusion at a token costs a task its place in the [[j-space]] altogether. A trial counts as reaching if the task's content hits lens rank 5 or better at any position in layers 16 to 22. Solid bars give the single-task rate, hatched the dual-task rate. Both concepts fall from 100% to 93%. The arithmetic answer falls further, 90% to 66%.

The computation, not the held concept, bears the cost of sharing, which is what a [[workspace-capacity-limit]] would predict for the harder of two loads.

terms.term: A: Example: the readout at two response tokens
terms.definition: The left panel's title. It prints two full prompts and, beneath each, the lens readout at two tokens of the model's copied response, as qualitative illustration rather than aggregate evidence.
The blue label for the first condition in panel A, in which the prompt instructs the model to concentrate on two unrelated concepts at once, citrus fruits and farm animals.

The orange label for the second condition in panel A, in which the prompt instructs the model to concentrate on one concept, citrus fruits, and to evaluate an arithmetic expression in its head at the same time.

A task the model is told to carry out mentally while writing something unrelated, so that no trace of it appears in the visible output. Both instructed items here are covert: the model writes only the copied sentence.

terms.term: "Write \"The old painting hung crookedly on the wall.\" ... Don't write anything else."
terms.definition: The prompt template, reproduced from the figure. The copied sentence is fixed across conditions, so the surface text is identical and any difference in the readouts comes from the instruction alone.
The concept named in both conditions, highlighted green in the prompt. Its content shows up in the readout as orange, orang, Orange, fruits and juice.
The second concept in the two-concepts condition, highlighted purple. Its content shows up as horses, animals, farms, livestock and farmers.
The arithmetic problem in the second condition, highlighted purple and printed in the figure with a caret. The model is told to evaluate it mentally while copying the sentence.
The line prefix marking the model's response in panel A. In both conditions the response is exactly the requested sentence, with no sign of either covert task.
One of the two response tokens the lens is applied at: the piece of "crookedly" shaded in the response line. It is a purely orthographic fragment, unrelated to either instructed task.
The other response token the lens is applied at, the word "on" in the copied sentence, also shaded in the response line and unrelated to either task.

The layer at which the panel-A readouts are taken, printed before each readout row. The paper's running text describes the same readouts at layer 75, so the figure's layer indices appear to follow a different numbering than the prose.
The list of vocabulary tokens the Jacobian lens ranks highest for a given activation, read as what that position is about. Each readout row in panel A is one such ranked list, printed left to right.

The paper's read technique: one vector per vocabulary token per layer, giving the direction that disposes the model toward saying that token, used here to score every token against the residual stream at a position.
The region of representation space spanned by sparse combinations of J-lens vectors, which the paper argues functions as a global workspace. Panels B and C measure how two tasks share it.
Marks readout tokens belonging to the first instructed item, citrus fruits in both conditions, and the matching phrase in the prompt.
Marks readout tokens belonging to the second instructed item: farm animals in the upper condition, the arithmetic values in the lower one.
The rank of that token in the lens top-10 at that position. Only task-relevant tokens carry a numeral, so the gaps in the numbering are the unhighlighted tokens sitting in between.

Non-English tokens appearing unhighlighted in the readouts, in Russian, Chinese, Japanese and Korean. They sit alongside the English thinking and answer words and belong to neither instructed task; the lens ranks over the whole tokenizer vocabulary, not over English alone.

terms.term: thinking, thoughts, thinks, mentally, thought, imag
terms.definition: Generic words for the act of thinking that fill the readout at "on" in the two-concepts condition and share ranks with the fruit words at "ook" in the other condition. The paper reads these as the model representing the fact of holding something in mind, separately from the content held.

terms.term: Nine, nine, seventeen, seven, Eight, ninete, Seven, eight, Answer
terms.definition: The readout at "on" in the concept-plus-arithmetic condition. It mixes the intermediate value nine, the final answer seven, and near-miss numbers, indicating the computation itself is occupying that token.
The middle panel's title. Co-occupancy is the rate at which the two tasks are present in the readout at the same token position.

terms.term: P(the other task is in the lens top-10) at tokens where this task is in the top-10
terms.definition: The y-axis of panel B. It conditions on the positions where one task's content is already in the top-10 of the readout, then measures how often the partner task's content is there as well.
The presence threshold used in panel B: a task counts as occupying a token if any of its content words falls among the ten highest-ranked lens tokens there.

The grey bars. The partner task's occupancy is measured on a different prompt, one where each instruction was given on its own, so the control gives the co-occupancy expected if the two tasks were placed independently.
The blue bar pair, for the condition where both instructed items are concepts.
The orange bar pair, for the condition pairing a held concept with an arithmetic computation.
The black whiskers on each bar in panel B, showing the uncertainty of each rate. The figure does not state which interval they represent.

terms.term: C: Reachability: single vs dual task
terms.definition: The right panel's title. Reachability asks whether a task's content makes it near the top of the lens anywhere in the response, rather than at any particular token.

terms.term: reaches lens top-5 (band L16-22, any position)
terms.definition: The y-axis of panel C, the fraction of trials on which the task's content attains lens rank 5 or better at some position and some layer in the given band. The paper's text gives this band as layers 67 to 92, again a different numbering.
The baseline condition of panel C: the instruction was given on its own, with no second covert task alongside it.
The condition of panel C in which the same instruction was given alongside the other task, so the two must share the workspace.
The blue group, tracking the concepts from the two-concepts condition.
The first orange group, tracking the held concept in the condition where the partner task is the arithmetic problem.
The second orange group, tracking whether the computed result of 3^2 - 2 reaches the top of the lens. This is the item that loses the most under dual load.
The workspace-like property this experiment extends: the model can put a named concept into the J-space on instruction, independently of what it writes.
The claim from global workspace theory that only a small selection of ongoing activity is held at once, so entry is competitive. The mutual exclusion in panel B is offered as an instance of it.

numbers.meaning: The arithmetic problem in the second condition and its answer. It is a two-step problem: square 3 to get 9, then subtract 2 to get 7. Both steps show up in the readout at "on", nine at ranks 1 to 3 and seven at ranks 4 and 7, which is why the paper describes the readout there as the computation in progress rather than a retrieved fact.

The layer of the panel-A readouts. It sits inside the middle band where the paper finds the J-space carrying workspace content, rather than in the early layers where it is nearly empty or the last layers where readouts turn into next-token predictions.

Ranks within the lens top-10 at that position. In the two-concepts readout at "ook" the marked ranks run orange 1, orange 2, horses 3, animals 4, Orange 6, farms 7, livestock 8, farmers 9, fruits 10, with rank 5 taken by an unhighlighted token; the alternation of green and purple is what the paper means by the two concepts interleaving.
The presence threshold in panel B. A task counts as occupying a token if any of its content reaches the ten highest-ranked lens tokens there; the co-occupancy rate is defined relative to this cutoff.

Co-occupancy for two held concepts: at tokens where one concept is in the top-10, the other is too on 46% of them. The paper reads this as the two concepts placing themselves without regard to each other.

The shuffled control for the two-concepts condition, measured on prompts where each instruction was given alone. Since 0.46 sits within error of 0.53, the observed sharing is what independent placement would produce, so nothing is competing.
Co-occupancy for a concept and a computed answer: they land on the same token 6% of the time. This is the panel's central number, an almost complete mutual exclusion.

The shuffled control for the concept-plus-math condition. The gap from 0.26 down to 0.06 is roughly a factor of four, and it is that gap, not the raw 0.06, that makes the exclusion a real effect rather than a consequence of each task being rare.
The y-axis range of panel B. Both observed bars and both controls sit in the lower half, so even in the two-concepts case most tokens carry only one task.

The values the appendix prose reports for the concept-plus-math bar and its control, against 0.06 and 0.26 printed in the figure. The qualitative claim, exclusion well below control, is the same either way, but the two sources do not agree on the exact rates.
The reachability threshold in panel C, stricter than the top-10 used for co-occupancy. A trial counts only if the task's content reaches rank 5 or better.

The layer band searched in panel C. Reachability is scored over any layer in this band and any position in the response, which is why its rates are much higher than the per-token co-occupancy rates of panel B. The prose names this band as layers 67 to 92.

Single-task reachability for the concepts, in both the two-concepts group and the concept-with-math group. A concept held on its own reaches the top of the lens somewhere in every trial, which sets the ceiling the dual-task bars are compared against.

Dual-task reachability for the concepts, in both groups. The drop from 100% is 7 points, so holding a second task alongside a concept costs that concept almost nothing at the level of the whole response.

Single-task reachability for the arithmetic answer. It starts below the concepts even without a partner task, which the paper does not explain; a multi-step computation is simply less reliable than holding a word in mind.

Dual-task reachability for the arithmetic answer, a fall of 24 points from 90%. This is the largest decline in the panel and the basis for the claim that the computation, not the concept, pays for sharing the workspace.

The values the appendix prose gives for the arithmetic answer's single- and dual-task reachability, against 90% and 66% in the figure. The size of the decline, roughly 23 to 24 points, agrees; the levels do not.
The y-axis range of panel C, with gridlines at 25, 50, 75 and 100 percent.
The number of covert tasks held at once throughout the figure, and the number of response tokens shown in panel A. The experiment tests only the two-task case; no larger load is reported.
